title: Performing Art Heritage in India
summary: Indian music has three broad forms: Hindustani (a blend of Indo-Turko-Persian styles), Carnatic (South Indian, linked to bhakti saints and temple rituals from the 8th century and the guru-shishya tradition) and folk music (of the common people and regions; Dom, Mirasi, Manganiar and Langa communities; in Kashmir Chhakri, Tambur Naghma and Bcha Naghma). Martial music was played in battles (Hapa Charan and Mian Lal Khan in Akbar's time; the Dadis of western Rajasthan; the sazindas of Kashmir).

Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), nicknamed Tuti-e-Hind (parrot of India), was born at Patiali, Etah (Uttar Pradesh), and was a disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya. He wrote that Indian music is 'the fire that burns heart and soul' and superior to any other country's. He blended Arabic, Persian and Indian music, is credited with Qawwali and Tarana and with inventing the sitar, and claimed all the ragas of Nayak Gopal as his own. Tansen (born in a Brahmin family of Gwalior) was a disciple of Haridas, served Raja Ram Chand of Baghelkhand and then Akbar, and is considered the composer of the Dhrupad form. Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri records that Sufi Shaikh Salim Chishti wished to hear Tansen sing at his death. The Gwalior (Seniya) Gharana and the Tansen Sangeet Sammelan in Gwalior attract tourists.

Flute (bansuri): a wind instrument in the Vedic texts, associated with Lord Krishna. Tanpura: long-necked string instrument that gives the basic note (4–5 wires). Tabla: percussion; Ustad Zakir Hussain won a Grammy in 1992. Veena: one of the oldest instruments; the Saraswati Veena of South India accompanies Carnatic music. Sitar: plucked, seven strings (five steel, two brass); Pt. Ravi Shankar won the Bharat Ratna in 1999 and three Grammys. Shehnai: aerophonic, played at North Indian weddings and processions; Ustad Bismillah Khan received the Bharat Ratna in 2001. Nagaswaram (Nadaswaram): very long, auspicious instrument of Tamil Nadu temples. Sarod: stringed, from the rebab; Ustad Amjad Ali Khan. Sarangi: bowed, from 'sau rang' (hundred colours), closest to the human voice. Santoor: trapezoid folk instrument of Kashmir played with mezrab (hammers), used in Sufiana kalam. Mridangam: literally 'body of clay', rhythm in Carnatic music (Khol in Bengal). Others: Gottuvadyam, Chenda (Kerala, for Kathakali and Koodiyattam), Rabab (the national instrument of the Arabs; Tansen's disciples were Rababiyas and Beenkaras), Dhol, Dholak, Dhak, Khanjira and Pakhawaj (used in Dhrupad).

Dance in India goes back to the Indus Valley (the torso of a male dancer from Harappa and the dancing girl of Mohenjodaro). It has classical forms (Bharatanatyam, Mohiniattam, Manipuri, Odissi, Kathakali, Kathak, Kuchipudi) and folk forms. Folk dances: Lai Haraoba (Manipur, 'festival of gods'), Karagam (Tamil Nadu, pitchers on heads), Jhika Dasain (Santhal, Jharkhand), Jagar (Kumaun and Garhwal), Bhaktaa (Mayurbhanj, Odisha), Garba (Gujarat, Navratri, 9 nights, around a lamp) and Dandiya (with sticks), Kavadi Aattam (Tamil Nadu, males, balancing a pole with pots), Gidda (Punjab, women only), Ghoomar (Rajasthan, developed by the Bhil tribe, worships goddess Saraswati), Lavani (Maharashtra, Tamasha, dholaki, nine-yard sari), Bihu (Assam), Morulem (Goa, Shigmo festival, peacock feathers), Bhangra (Punjab, harvest, dhol and chimta) and Kalbelia (Rajasthan, snake charmers' tribe).

Drama has dialogue, music and dance (Sanskrit nata, nataka, natya; from nrit, 'to dance'). Its oldest treatise is Bharata's Natyashastra (the fifth Veda). The stage is technically Jarjara, linked to the flag staff of Indra that kept demons away from the performance. Forms: stage performance, street theatre (street corners, socio-political; Tavernier's account of jugglers on the Agra–Surat road), puppet shows and Nukkad Natak (street play on social issues; Safdar Hashmi, Jan Natya Manch).

Puppetry (from Latin pupa, 'doll'; Silappadikaram, 2nd century BC; themes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata): string puppets (Rajasthan, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka), shadow puppets (flat leather figures behind a lit screen; Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka), glove puppets (hand puppets controlled by fingers) and rod puppets (bigger, from below; West Bengal and Odisha).

vsa: Describe any two characteristics of the musical instrument 'Veena'.
It is one of the oldest instruments, mentioned in the Vedic texts. The Saraswati Veena of South India is a plucked string instrument of the lute family used to accompany Carnatic music.
October 2025

or: Describe any two characteristics of the musical instrument 'Shehnai'.
It is an aerophonic tube-like instrument that widens towards the lower end. It is played at North Indian weddings and processions, and Ustad Bismillah Khan made it famous.

vsa: Describe any two characteristics of the musical instrument 'Sarangi'.
It is a bowed string instrument, and its name comes from sau (hundred) and rang (colour). It is very close to the human voice, so it is regarded as the best accompanying instrument.
April 2025
Write a short note on Carnatic music.

Carnatic music is the music of South India and is linked with devotion to God and temple rituals from the 8th century. Bhakti saints sang praise of God, and the guru-shishya tradition gave it a prime place in musicology.
April 2025

or: Write a short note on Indian theatre.

Indian theatre goes back to the Vedas, and drama has dialogue, music and dance. Its forms are stage performance, street theatre, puppet shows and Nukkad Natak, with Bharata's Natyashastra as the oldest treatise.

vsa: Distinguish between a 'shadow puppet' and a 'glove puppet'.
Shadow puppets are flat leather figures pressed against a screen with light behind to make shadows. Glove puppets are hand puppets controlled by the puppeteer's fingers inside them.

Mention the incident about Tansen recorded in the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.
It records that the Sufi Shaikh Salim Chishti of Fatehpur Sikri, at the time of his death, expressed the last wish to hear Tansen sing. Jahangir calls Tansen 'unequalled as a singer'.
October 2024
Write a short note on Bihu.
Bihu is the dance of the Bihu festival of Assam. Men and women take part to traditional Bihu music, and it has forms such as the Deori and Mising Bihu.
April 2024
Write a short note on Morulem.
Morulem is the traditional folk dance of Goa performed during the Shigmo festival. It is named after 'mor' (peacock), the dancers wear peacock feathers and garlands, and it invokes the deities.
What is Nukkad Natak?
It is a form of street play that carries socio-political themes to create awareness about contemporary issues. Safdar Hashmi and groups like Jan Natya Manch made it popular.
Write any two features of the Santoor.
It is a trapezoid-shaped folk instrument of Kashmir made of walnut wood with many strings. It is played with two light hammers (mezrab) and is used in Sufiana kalam.
What are the Dadis?
They are a community of western Rajasthan whose profession was to accompany rulers in battle and encourage the soldiers. Their style of music was known as Sindhu singing.
sa: Analyse any three main features of the musical instrument associated with Lord Krishna (the flute).

(i) The flute (bansuri) is a wind instrument that makes sound from air flowing across an opening, and it is mentioned in the Vedic texts. (ii) It appears in the sculptures of Sanchi and Amaravati and the paintings of Ajanta and Ellora. (iii) Its volume can be increased by enlarging the resonator and tone holes, and it has also become a part of Western orchestra.
Write short notes on any two folk dances of India.

(i) Garba (Gujarat) is danced around a lit lamp or the goddess Shakti for nine nights during Navratri. (ii) Kalbelia (Rajasthan) is danced by the snake-catching Kalbelia tribe with serpent-like movements by both men and women. Dandiya is danced with sticks.
Explain the contribution of the folk dances to tourism in India (three points).

(i) Festival dances such as Garba and Bihu draw large crowds of visitors. (ii) Folk dances show the regional culture and keep traditions alive. (iii) They give tourists direct cultural experience through melas and festivals.
Describe the different forms of puppetry in India (three points).

(i) String puppets have jointed limbs controlled by strings (Rajasthan, Odisha). (ii) Shadow puppets are flat leather figures shown against a lit screen (Andhra Pradesh, Kerala), and glove puppets are worn on the hand. (iii) Rod puppets are larger and controlled from below (West Bengal, Odisha).
Explain how Hindustani music differs from Carnatic and folk music (three points).

(i) Hindustani music of North India is a blend of Indo-Turko-Persian styles. (ii) Carnatic music of South India grew from bhakti and temple rituals. (iii) Folk music belongs to the common people and regions and is sung at melas, festivals and marriages.
la: Explain the contribution of Amir Khusrau to Indian music in six points.

(i) He was nicknamed Tuti-e-Hind and learned Arabic, Persian and Indian music. (ii) He blended Arabic and Persian music with Indian music, adding grace to it. (iii) He is credited with inventing Qawwali and Tarana. (iv) He is said to have invented the sitar and wrote three volumes of musical compositions. (v) He faced Nayak Gopal in Alauddin's court and claimed all the ragas Gopal sang had been invented by him, mingling the music of North and South. (vi) He wrote that Indian music is 'the fire that burns heart and soul' and was a disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya.

or: Explain the contribution of Tansen to music in six points.

(i) He was born in a Brahmin family in Gwalior and was a disciple of Haridas. (ii) He served in the court of Raja Ram Chand of Baghelkhand. (iii) Akbar heard of him and called him to the court, rewarding him with two krors of dams. (iv) He is considered the composer of the Dhrupad form. (v) Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri records that Sufi Salim Chishti wished to hear him sing. (vi) The Gwalior (Seniya) Gharana traces its link to him and the Tansen Sangeet Sammelan at Gwalior draws tourists.

la: Describe the different musical instruments of India and their famous players, in six points.

(i) Flute and Tanpura: the flute is linked to Krishna and the tanpura gives the basic note. (ii) Tabla (Zakir Hussain) and Mridangam (Carnatic rhythm). (iii) Sitar (Ravi Shankar, Bharat Ratna 1999) and Sarod (Amjad Ali Khan). (iv) Shehnai (Bismillah Khan, Bharat Ratna 2001) and Nagaswaram (Tamil Nadu temples). (v) Veena (the oldest, Carnatic), Sarangi (like the human voice) and Santoor (Kashmir). (vi) Others: Chenda, Rabab, Dhol, Khanjira and Pakhawaj.
Explain the evolution of folk and classical dance and theatre in India, in six points.

(i) Dance is traceable to the Indus Valley, shown by the male torso of Harappa and the dancing girl of Mohenjodaro. (ii) Medieval times had classical dances for the elite and folk dances for the common people in melas and bazaars. (iii) Temple devdasis danced to please God. (iv) Folk dances include Garba, Bhangra and Bihu. (v) Drama grew from dance, with music added, and Bharata's Natyashastra is its oldest treatise. (vi) Street theatre, puppetry and Nukkad Natak carry the heritage of public performance.
